topics.title: Agentic Patterns
topics.titleHtml: Agentic Patterns
topics.search: 🚀 starting point starting point. a workflow runs model calls along a path you wrote in code. an agent lets the model choose the path: it decides which tool to call next, sees the result, and repeats until it decides it’s done. agents trade predictability for flexibility, so start with the simplest workflow that works and add autonomy only where the path can’t be known in advance. workflows augmented llm : one call with retrieval, tools and memory. the building block of everything else. prompt chaining : fixed sequence of calls with programmatic checks (“gates”) between them. routing : classify the input, send it to a specialised prompt or a cheaper model. parallelisation : sectioning (independent sub-tasks at once) or voting (the same task several times; self-consistency, multiple reviewers). orchestrator–workers : a lead model splits the task at run time and delegates to workers, then merges. evaluator–optimiser : one call drafts, another critiques against criteria, loop until it passes. react: reason, act, observe ⚙️ algorithm: react agent loop input: goal \(g\) , tools \(\mathcal t\) , step limit \(s\) , verifier \(v\) context \(\gets\) system prompt + tool descriptions + memory files + \(g\) for \(s=1,\dots,s\) do model reads context, writes a thought and either a tool call \((t,\text{args})\) or a final answer if final answer then if \(v\) passes then return answer else append “verification failed: …” and continue end end check \(t\in\mathcal t\) , validate args, check p

topics.title: Context Engineering
topics.titleHtml: Context Engineering
heads: Four moves: write, select, compress, isolate
topics.search: 🚀 starting point starting point. prompt engineering is writing one good message. context engineering is deciding everything the model sees at each step of a long run: system prompt, tool definitions, memory files, retrieved documents, conversation history, tool outputs and its own notes. the window is finite, attention over it is uneven, and every token is paid for on every call. real-life version: a desk. a clean desk with the three documents you need beats a desk buried under every document you own, even if the right one is somewhere in the pile. four moves: write, select, compress, isolate write context outside the window: scratchpads, progress files, todo lists, memory files ( agents.md ), git commits. the agent can re-read them after a reset. select what goes in: retrieval (bm25, embeddings, or the agent’s own grep and file reads, often called just-in-time retrieval), tool definitions relevant to this task, the right memory entries. compress : truncate tool outputs, clear old tool results once acted on, summarise (compact) the history when it grows past a threshold, keep identifiers (paths, urls) so details can be fetched again. isolate : give a sub-task to a subagent with a fresh context, run tools in a sandbox whose full output never enters the window, split state across agents. why less is more long contexts degrade gradually: models retrieve facts from the start and end of a long input better than from the middle ( lost in the middle ), accuracy on retrieval and reas

topics.titleHtml: AGENTS.md: Memory Files That Work
topics.search: 🚀 starting point agents.md is a plain markdown file at the root of a repository that tells coding agents what a new teammate would need on day one: how to build and test, the conventions, and the traps. it is an open convention read by several agents (codex, cursor, and others); claude code reads claude.md and gemini cli gemini.md , which can simply point to or import agents.md . the harness loads it into the context at the start of every session, so it is the one piece of context you fully control. what belongs in it # agents.md ## commands - install: `uv sync` - test: `make test` (single file: `pytest tests/test_x.py -q`) - lint/format: `make lint` - type check: `make typecheck` run test + lint before saying a task is done. ## layout - src/api/ fastapi routes; one file per resource - src/core/ business logic, no i/o - db/migrations generated with `make new-migration name=<slug>`, never edited by hand ## conventions - type hints on public functions; errors are raised as apperror subclasses (src/core/errors.py). - new endpoints need a test in tests/api/ using the `client` fixture. ## gotchas - integration tests need docker running (they start postgres). - `config/flags.yaml` is read at startup: restart the server after changing it. ## boundaries - do not modify files under vendor/ or .github/workflows/ without asking. - never commit secrets; .env is local only. practices short and specific. every line is read on every task and costs context. exact commands beat descriptions;

topics.title: Working with Frontier Models
topics.titleHtml: Working with Frontier Models
topics.search: 🚀 starting point frontier models (the latest claude, gpt and gemini families) follow instructions literally, reason internally before answering, call tools in parallel, and can work for hours on one task. most old prompting tricks are unnecessary; what matters is the brief, the tools, the checks and the context. brief like a senior colleague : the goal, why it matters, the constraints, what done looks like, and what to do when blocked. explicit beats implied: if you want the model to make changes rather than suggest them, say so. let it think : set the reasoning effort or thinking budget for hard tasks instead of writing “think step by step”. ask it to plan before large changes. give verification : tests, a script that checks the output, screenshots for ui. a model that can check its work iterates to correct; one that can’t stops at plausible. good tools : few, general, well-named tools with typed schemas and descriptions that say when to use them; errors that tell the model how to recover. let independent calls run in parallel. structured outputs via the api’s schema mode, not “reply in json please”. state in files for long work : a progress log, a todo list and git commits, so work survives context resets and can be resumed by a fresh session. subagents for breadth : searching a large codebase or the web in parallel keeps the lead agent’s context clean. calm instructions : no all caps or “you must”. strong models over-apply emphasised rules; one clear sentence with a reason

topics.search: 🚀 starting point a modern llm is built in stages. each stage uses the same next-token machinery from llm fundamentals , but different data and a different objective: pre-training (trillions of web tokens, learn language and knowledge), mid-training (higher-quality and longer data, sharpen skills), supervised fine-tuning (conversations, learn to follow instructions), preference optimization (pairs of better/worse answers, learn taste), and rl with verifiable rewards (problems with checkable answers, learn to reason). synthetic data made by other llms now feeds every one of them. the stages in order. compute is spent overwhelmingly on the left; behaviour is shaped mostly on the right. ✏️ derivation: how big a run can a budget buy? step 1. training flops \(c\approx6nd\) : \(n\) parameters, \(d\) tokens. every token costs about \(2n\) flops forward and \(4n\) backward ( llm fundamentals , session 10). step 2. a gpu delivers \(\text{mfu}\times\text{peak}\) useful flop/s. an h100’s dense bf16 peak is \(989\times10^{12}\) flop/s, and good runs reach 35–50% mfu. step 3. wall time \(=\dfrac{6nd}{\text{mfu}\cdot\text{peak}\cdot\#\text{gpus}}\) . step 4. this book’s pre-training run (chapter 5): \(n\approx123\) m, \(d=328\) m tokens: \(6\cdot1.23\times10^8\cdot3.28\times10^8=2.4\times10^{17}\) flops. at 40% mfu on one h100: \(2.4\times10^{17}/(0.4\cdot9.89\times10^{14})\approx610\) s, about 10 minutes of pure compute. step 5. a chinchilla-sized version ( \(d=20n=2.5\) b tokens) is \(7.5

topics.titleHtml: Tokenization: Training a BPE Tokenizer
topics.search: 🚀 starting point a tokenizer maps text to integer ids. byte-pair encoding starts from the 256 possible bytes (so any text can be encoded) and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, until the vocabulary reaches its target size. common words become single tokens; rare words stay as several pieces. ✏️ derivation: why vocabulary size is a trade-off step 1. compression \(c\) = bytes per token. english text with a 50k–150k vocabulary gets about 4–4.5 bytes per token. a fixed amount of text costs \(\text{bytes}/c\) tokens, so better compression means more text per flop and longer effective context. step 2. cost of a bigger vocabulary: the embedding and output layers have \(vd\) parameters each. for \(v=128\) k, \(d=4096\) : 524m parameters per matrix, a big share of a small model. the softmax also costs \(o(v)\) per token. step 3. rare tokens: a token seen only a few times during training gets a poorly trained embedding, so very large vocabularies need very large datasets. step 4. typical choices: gpt-2 50k, smollm2 49k, llama 3 128k, gemma 4 262k (multilingual), qwen3.8 248k. topics.titleHtml: Scaling Out: Data Parallelism, FSDP and Friends
topics.search: 🚀 starting point one gpu runs out of either memory or time. data parallelism copies the model to every gpu and splits the batch. sharding (zero / fsdp) splits the model’s state across gpus, so each holds \(1/g\) . tensor and pipeline parallelism split the model’s computation when even a sharded layer is too big or too slow. training state for an 8b model on 8 gpus (16 bytes/parameter, activations excluded). only full sharding gets it to 16 gb per gpu. ✏️ derivation: what fsdp communicates step 1. ddp: each gpu computes gradients on its own batch, then an all-reduce averages them. ring all-reduce sends about \(2\phi\) bytes per gpu for a gradient of \(\phi\) bytes, independent of \(g\) . step 2. fsdp: before a block’s forward, all-gather its weight shards into a full copy; free it after. backward: all-gather again, compute gradients, then reduce-scatter , so each gpu ends up with the summed gradient for its own shard only. each gpu then updates only its shard. step 3. volume per step \(\approx\phi\) (all-gather forward) \(+\phi\) (all-gather backward) \(+\phi\) (reduce-scatter) \(=3\phi\) : 1.5 \(\times\) ddp’s traffic, in exchange for \(g\times\) less memory. step 4. the traffic overlaps with compute: fsdp prefetches block \(\ell+1\) ’s weights while block \(\ell\) computes. that’s why it shards per block ( fully_shard(blk) in the code), not the whole model at once. step 5. when fsdp isn’t enough: tensor parallelism splits each matrix multiply across gpus inside a node (fast

topics.title: Mid-Training: Annealing, Data Mixtures and Long Context
topics.titleHtml: Mid-Training: Annealing, Data Mixtures and Long Context
topics.search: 🚀 starting point mid-training is the last part of pre-training, run with a different data mix: more math, code, textbooks and synthetic reasoning, plus some instruction-style text, during the learning-rate decay. it’s also where the context window is extended. most 2025–2026 base models are mid-trained before any post-training starts. ✏️ derivation: why the decay phase is the place for the best data step 1. during the constant-lr phase, the optimizer is noisy: each step moves the weights by about \(\eta\) in a direction dominated by gradient noise. loss falls slowly. step 2. as \(\eta\to0\) , the noise averages out and the weights settle into a sharper point of the basin. most of the final loss improvement happens here, and the model is most influenced by the data it sees last . step 3. so the recipe is: mostly web text in the stable phase, then switch to a high-quality mix for the 10–20% decay. olmo 2 calls this its “dolmino” mix; smollm2 and smollm3 use several stages with growing math and code shares. step 4. data mixtures: the mix is a set of weights over sources. small proxy runs (a few hundred million parameters) are used to choose them, because mixture preferences transfer reasonably well upward in scale. step 5. context extension: train on long documents with a larger rope base or yarn scaling ( llm fundamentals , part vi, “long context”), usually 4k/8k \(\to\) 32k–128k over a few billion tokens. deepseek-v4 extends 64k \(\to\) 1m with yarn factor 16; kimi k3 goes 8k

topics.search: 🚀 starting point after sft, the model follows instructions but its answers vary in quality. preference data pairs a prompt with a chosen and a rejected response. dpo raises the chosen response’s log-probability relative to a frozen reference model and lowers the rejected one’s, with no reward model and no sampling (derivation: llm fundamentals , session 26). ✏️ derivation: reading dpo’s training logs step 1. trl logs the implicit rewards \(\hat r^\pm=\beta\big(\log\pi_\theta(y^\pm|x)-\log\pi_{\text{ref}}(y^\pm|x)\big)\) . step 2. rewards/margins \(=\overline{\hat r^+-\hat r^-}\) . it starts at 0 (policy = reference) and should grow. step 3. rewards/accuracies = fraction of pairs with \(\hat r^+>\hat r^-\) . starts near 0.5. step 4. loss \(=\overline{\softplus(-(\hat r^+-\hat r^-))}\) , starting at \(\ln2=0.693\) . step 5. watch out: \(\hat r^+\) often goes down too (both responses become less likely, the rejected one more so). mild is normal; large drops in \(\hat r^+\) mean the model is drifting toward degenerate text, so lower the learning rate or raise \(\beta\) . topics.title: Distillation, Merging and Evaluation
topics.titleHtml: Distillation, Merging and Evaluation
topics.search: 🚀 starting point three last steps before shipping. distillation trains a small model on a big one’s outputs (offline, as sft on teacher samples) or its per-token distribution (on-policy, rl book topic 180; trl’s gkdtrainer and distillationtrainer ). merging averages fine-tuned weights. evaluation measures the result on benchmarks the model never saw. ✏️ derivation: why averaging weights can work step 1. fine-tuning moves weights by a task vector \(\tau_i=\theta_i-\theta_{\text{base}}\) , usually small relative to \(\theta_{\text{base}}\) . step 2. near the base, the loss is roughly quadratic, and two fine-tunes from the same base sit in the same basin. averaging \(\theta_{\text{base}}+\frac1k\sum\tau_i\) often keeps most of each task’s gain (model soups, task arithmetic). step 3. it fails when task vectors interfere: ties and dare first drop small or sign-conflicting entries of each \(\tau_i\) , then merge. step 4. it never works across different bases: weights from separate pre-training runs aren’t aligned neuron by neuron. evaluation checklist (with lighteval or lm-evaluation-harness ): decontaminate first (chapter 3), against every reported benchmark. use the model’s chat template and the same generation settings for every model compared. report pass@1 with several samples and a confidence interval ( llm fundamentals , sessions 43–44), plus pass@ \(k\) if you’ll deploy with retries. keep a held-out set that you never look at during development, for the final number.

topics.search: 🚀 starting point a reward model (rm) is a language model with its output layer replaced by a single number. it’s trained on preference pairs with the bradley–terry loss \(-\log\sigma(r^+-r^-)\) ( llm fundamentals , session 36) and then used three ways: as the reward in ppo-style rlhf, to pick the best of \(n\) samples, and to label new preference pairs for dpo. ✏️ derivation: why trl adds a centering term step 1. bradley–terry only sees differences: replacing \(r(x,y)\) with \(r(x,y)+c(x)\) leaves the loss unchanged, so the scores’ offset drifts freely during training. step 2. a drifting offset is harmless for ranking but harmful for rl, where the absolute scale of the reward sets the effective kl strength (rl book, topic 127). step 3. center_rewards_coefficient \(=\lambda\) adds \(\lambda\,\overline{(r^++r^-)^2}\) , which pulls the mean score toward 0 without changing which response wins. trl recommends \(\lambda=0.01\) . step 4. ensembles (several rms, use the mean minus a multiple of their spread) reduce reward hacking but don’t eliminate it: members trained on the same data share blind spots (rl book, topics 130–131). ✏️ derivation: two reward models instead of one step 1. pku-saferlhf labels each response pair twice: which is more helpful and which is safer . these often disagree: the safer answer is frequently a refusal. step 2. training one rm on a mix of both labels forces it to pick one exchange rate between helpfulness and harmlessness, baked into the weights. step

topics.title: Why Synthetic Data, and How It Can Go Wrong
topics.titleHtml: Why Synthetic Data, and How It Can Go Wrong
topics.search: 🚀 starting point synthetic data is training data written by an llm. it has gone from a trick to the default: smoltalk and tulu 3’s sft mixes are mostly synthetic, nemotron-cc-v2 includes about 2.5t tokens of llm-rephrased web text, and almost every open reasoning model is trained on traces sampled from a stronger one. it’s cheap, controllable and scalable. its risks are low diversity , inherited errors , and model collapse when models train on their own outputs. every synthetic-data recipe in this part has these four stages. the filter is where quality comes from. ✏️ derivation: model collapse in one line of math step 1. fit a gaussian to \(n\) samples, sample \(n\) new points from the fit, refit, repeat. each refit’s variance estimate \(\hat\sigma^2_{t+1}\) is \(\hat\sigma^2_t\cdot\chi^2_{n-1}/(n-1)\) , a random factor with mean slightly below 1 for the usual mle. step 2. products of such factors drift toward 0: tails disappear first, then variance collapses (shumailov et al., 2024). the llm version: rare facts and styles vanish after a few generations of training on outputs. step 3. mitigation: accumulate rather than replace. keep the real data and add synthetic data each round; under this regime the error stays bounded (gerstgrasser et al., 2024). in practice: mix synthetic with real data, filter hard, and generate from diverse seeds.

topics.search: 🚀 starting point three ways to use an llm to make pre-training data: generate textbooks from topic seeds, rephrase real web pages into cleaner or more varied forms, or extract question–answer pairs from them. rephrasing is the most popular now because the facts come from real documents while the style and density come from the model. phi-1 / “textbooks are all you need” (microsoft, 2023): about 1b tokens of gpt-3.5 textbooks and exercises, plus filtered code, let a 1.3b model beat much larger ones on humaneval. cosmopedia (huggingface, 2024): about 25b tokens (30m files) of synthetic textbooks, blog posts and stories from mixtral-8x7b-instruct, seeded by web pages and curated topic lists, for diversity. cosmopedia v2 is part of smollm-corpus . wrap (apple/cmu, 2024): rephrase web documents “like wikipedia” or “as question–answer”; mixing rephrased with real data trains about 3 \(\times\) faster to the same perplexity. nemotron-cc-v2 (nvidia, 2025; dataset card read this week): 3.36t tokens of real english crawl, plus 1.26t tokens of synthetic rephrasings and 0.69t of “diverse qa” (also translated into 15 languages, 0.56t), generated with mistral-nemo-12b and qwen3-30b-a3b using five prompt styles. the rephrase function in synth.py (listing in the next chapter) does this with three prompts: wiki , qa and textbook . mix its output with the original documents rather than replacing them.

topics.title: What Alignment Means in Post-Training
topics.titleHtml: What Alignment Means in Post-Training
topics.search: 🚀 starting point alignment is getting a model to do what its developers and users intend: be helpful , honest and harmless (the “hhh” framing). in practice it’s an engineering loop: write down the intended behaviour (a spec or constitution ), turn it into data, train on that data, and evaluate whether the model follows it, including in cases nobody wrote down. constitutional ai (anthropic, 2022): the model critiques and revises its own outputs against written principles (giving sft data), and an ai judge applies the principles to label preference pairs (rlaif). code in the next chapter. deliberative alignment (openai, 2024, as i recall it): train the model to recall the relevant part of the spec in its reasoning and apply it before answering, using sft on spec-citing reasoning and then rl with a spec-aware judge. the trade-off is real: every refusal of a harmful request risks refusing a similar benign one. a safety result means nothing without its over-refusal rate.

topics.title: Safety Training: Data, Refusals and Constraints
topics.titleHtml: Safety Training: Data, Refusals and Constraints
topics.search: 🚀 starting point safety post-training uses the same trainers as everything else, with safety data in the mix: harmful requests with good refusals or safe completions , benign requests that look risky with helpful answers (to prevent over-refusal), and preference pairs where the safer response wins. a safe completion helps with the legitimate part of a request (“how do i store medication safely around kids”) instead of refusing everything near the topic. ✏️ derivation: safe rlhf: helpfulness subject to a harm budget step 1. train two models (chapter 12): reward \(r(x,y)\) for helpfulness and cost \(c(x,y)\) for harm. step 2. objective: \(\max_\pi\ \mathbb e[r]\) subject to \(\mathbb e[c]\le d\) . a single blended reward \(r-\lambda c\) with a fixed \(\lambda\) can’t guarantee the constraint. step 3. lagrangian: \(\mathcal l(\pi,\lambda)=\mathbb e[r]-\lambda(\mathbb e[c]-d)\) , \(\lambda\ge0\) . alternate a policy step on \(r-\lambda c\) with \(\lambda\gets\max(0,\lambda+\eta(\hat c-d))\) (rl book, topic 151). step 4. \(\lambda\) rises while the policy is too harmful and falls once it’s within budget, so the exchange rate between helpfulness and harmlessness is set by the data, not guessed. topics.search: 🚀 starting point a guard model is a separate classifier that reads a prompt (input moderation) or a prompt plus response (output moderation) and returns a verdict. it lets a deployment enforce policy without retraining the main model, and it can be updated faster. most guards today are small llms that generate their verdict. qwen3guard (qwen, october 2025; model card read this month): 0.6b, 4b and 8b. the gen variants output safety: safe | unsafe | controversial , a list of categories (violent, non-violent illegal acts, sexual content, pii, suicide & self-harm, unethical acts, politically sensitive topics, copyright violation, and jailbreak for inputs), and for responses refusal: yes | no . the stream variants add a per-token head to moderate output while it’s generated. controversial lets you choose a strict or loose policy at deployment. guard model (hf id) access notes qwen/qwen3guard-gen-0.6b (4b, 8b) open three severity levels, refusal detection, streaming variant meta-llama/llama-guard-4-12b gated multimodal, mlcommons hazard taxonomy allenai/wildguard gated prompt harm, response harm and refusal in one pass google/shieldgemma-2b gated policy-conditioned yes/no probability ibm-granite/granite-guardian-3.3-8b open harm plus rag groundedness and hallucination checks ✏️ derivation: layers help, but less than multiplication suggests step 1. let layer \(i\) miss a given harmful exchange with probability \(m_i\) : an input guard, the model’s own refusal, an output guard. step

topics.title: Measuring Safety: Attack Success and Over-Refusal
topics.titleHtml: Measuring Safety: Attack Success and Over-Refusal
topics.search: 🚀 starting point two numbers, always together. attack success rate (asr): the fraction of harmful prompts that get a harmful answer, as judged by a guard or human. over-refusal : the fraction of benign prompts that get refused. a model that refuses everything has asr 0 and is useless; a model that refuses nothing has over-refusal 0 and is unsafe. ✏️ derivation: the trade-off is an roc curve step 1. suppose the model (or a guard) refuses when its harm score \(s\) exceeds a threshold \(\tau\) . step 2. \(\text{asr}(\tau)=p(s<\tau\mid\text{harmful})\) falls as \(\tau\) falls; \(\text{or}(\tau)=p(s\ge\tau\mid\text{benign})\) rises as \(\tau\) falls. step 3. plotting one against the other as \(\tau\) varies traces an roc-style curve. moving along it trades one error for the other. only a better score (better training, better guard) moves the curve itself. step 4. so compare models at matched over-refusal, or report the whole curve. a paper reporting “lower asr” without over-refusal hasn’t shown improvement. step 5. use matched benign prompts on the same topics (jailbreakbench pairs 100 harmful with 100 benign behaviours; xstest has 250 safe prompts that look unsafe), and report bootstrap intervals: with 100 prompts, \(\pm6\) points is typical. topics.title: Red Teaming and Why Safety Training Is Fragile
topics.titleHtml: Red Teaming and Why Safety Training Is Fragile
topics.search: 🚀 starting point red teaming searches for inputs that make a model violate its policy, so they can be fixed before users find them. it’s done by people, by other llms (automated red teaming), and by optimization. the findings feed back into safety data and guard training. this chapter is about defending: what the main failure patterns are and why they work. attack families defenders test for: role-play and fictional framing; many-shot prompts (a long context full of fake compliant examples); encoding or translation into low-resource languages; multi-turn escalation; optimized adversarial suffixes (gcg, 2023); and prompt injection, where instructions hidden in a tool result or document hijack an agent. each has public benchmarks, and a release should report results on each family. ✏️ derivation: why “shallow” safety breaks step 1. refusal training mostly changes the first few response tokens: harmful prompt \(\rightarrow\) “i can’t help with that.” later tokens’ distribution, conditioned on a compliant start, changes much less. step 2. so an attack only needs to get the first tokens wrong: prefilling “sure, here is”, or a framing that makes a compliant opening likely. after that the model continues from its pre-trained distribution. step 3. the same reasoning explains fine-tuning erosion : a few hundred gradient steps on unrelated data can move those first-token probabilities back. several 2026 papers study this (e.g. “a gravitational interpretation of safety reversion under f

topics.titleHtml: Failure Modes of Post-Training
topics.search: 🚀 starting point optimization finds whatever the training signal rewards, including things nobody intended. these are the failure modes post-training teams test for most often. the dates and findings below are from published work as i remember it, so check the papers before citing. reward hacking : the policy exploits reward-model or verifier errors (rl book, topics 33, 58–59). watch reward rising while held-out quality doesn’t. sycophancy : agreeing with the user, flattering, or changing a correct answer under pushback (anthropic, 2023; meg-tong/sycophancy-eval on the hub). alignment faking (anthropic/redwood, 2024): in experiments, a model behaved differently when it believed it was being trained versus not. sleeper agents (anthropic, 2024): deliberately backdoored behaviour survived standard safety training. emergent misalignment (2025): fine-tuning on a narrow bad behaviour (insecure code) produced broadly misaligned answers elsewhere. 2026 follow-ups include “unintended side effects of value training in llms” (arxiv 2610.29922) and “aligned data can induce misalignment via context confusion” (arxiv 2609.38379). ✏️ derivation: how rater bias becomes sycophancy step 1. suppose that between two answers of equal quality, human raters prefer the one that agrees with the user’s stated view with probability \(q>0.5\) . step 2. bradley–terry fits \(\sigma(r_{\text{agree}}-r_{\text{disagree}})=q\) , so the reward model learns an agreement bonus \(\delta r=\log\frac{q}{1-q}\) . fo

topics.title: Interpretability for Safety: Probes and Monitors
topics.titleHtml: Interpretability for Safety: Probes and Monitors
topics.search: 🚀 starting point interpretability looks inside the model. for safety, the most practical tools are linear probes : small classifiers on hidden states that detect a property (“this request is harmful,” “this reasoning is deceptive”) before or during generation. they’re cheap to run next to the model and give a signal that doesn’t depend on its final text. ✏️ derivation: the best linear probe for gaussian classes step 1. model hidden states as \(h\sim\mathcal n(\mu_+,\sigma)\) for harmful and \(\mathcal n(\mu_-,\sigma)\) for benign, with a shared covariance. step 2. log-odds: \(\log\frac{p(+|h)}{p(-|h)}=-\tfrac12(h-\mu_+)^\top\sigma^{-1}(h-\mu_+)+\tfrac12(h-\mu_-)^\top\sigma^{-1}(h-\mu_-)+\text{const}\) . the quadratic terms in \(h\) cancel. step 3. what’s left is linear: \(w^\top h+b\) with \(\boxed{w=\sigma^{-1}(\mu_+-\mu_-)}\) . that’s fisher’s lda. step 4. if \(\sigma\propto i\) , \(w\propto\mu_+-\mu_-\) : the simple difference-of-means probe is optimal. with correlated noise it isn’t, because lda down-weights directions where noise is large. step 5. the output below shows this: with correlated noise, difference of means reaches 54% and lda 93%, even though the lda direction is less aligned with the planted signal. the optimal direction isn’t the signal direction; it’s the signal “whitened” by the noise. topics.search: 👋 intro what system design is, how to measure a system (latency, throughput, availability), how systems scale, the cap and pacelc theorems, consistency models, and back-of-the-envelope estimation. what is system design? 🌱 beginner imagine opening a small restaurant. on day one, one cook takes orders, cooks, and serves. when 500 people show up, you need more cooks (scaling), a waiter to hand out orders (load balancer), pre-made sauces (cache), a ticket rail for orders (queue), and a backup generator (redundancy). system design is planning the restaurant before the crowd arrives. every design starts from two kinds of requirements: functional requirements : what the system does (“users can post a photo”). non-functional requirements : how well it does it: latency, availability, durability, consistency, cost, security, compliance. non-functional requirements drive almost every architectural decision. measuring a system 🔧 intermediate latency : time for one request. always report percentiles (p50, p95, p99, p99.9), never just averages. throughput : work per unit time (qps, tokens/s, mb/s). availability : fraction of time the system serves correctly. durability : probability data is never lost (s3: 11 nines). sli / slo / sla : the indicator you measure (p99 latency), the internal objective (p99 \(<\) 200 ms for 99.9% of minutes), and the external agreement with penalties. the “nines” of availability availability downtime / year downtime / month 99% (two nines) 3.65 days 7.3 hours 9

topics.search: 👋 intro asynchronous communication: queues vs pub/sub, kafka’s log model, delivery guarantees, ordering, dead-letter queues, event-driven architecture, event sourcing, cqrs, the outbox pattern, and change data capture. why asynchronous? 🌱 beginner calling someone on the phone is synchronous: both of you must be free at the same time. sending a text is asynchronous: you send it, carry on, and they reply when ready. message queues are text messages between services. if the receiver is busy or down, the message waits instead of being lost. benefits: decoupling (producer does not know the consumer), load leveling (absorb spikes), resilience (consumer outages do not fail the user’s request), and fan-out (many consumers react to one event). message queues (point-to-point) competing consumers: each message goes to exactly one worker. poison messages land in a dead-letter queue. 🔧 intermediate key mechanics: acknowledgement : the consumer acks after processing. no ack within the visibility timeout means redelivery. dead-letter queue (dlq) : messages that fail \(n\) times are moved aside for inspection rather than blocking the queue. delivery guarantees : at-most-once (ack before processing, may lose), at-least-once (ack after, may duplicate; the common default), and effectively-once (at-least-once plus idempotent consumers). ordering : standard sqs is best-effort; sqs fifo and kafka partitions give order per group/key. backpressure : queue depth is the signal for autoscaling workers

topics.search: 👋 intro why transactions across services are hard, two-phase commit, the saga pattern (choreography and orchestration), durable execution engines, and consensus algorithms like raft. the problem 🌱 beginner booking a holiday needs a flight, a hotel, and a car. if the car rental fails after you paid for the flight and hotel, you want all three cancelled, not a flight to a city where you have nowhere to sleep. inside one database, a transaction gives this “all or nothing” for free. across three companies’ systems, you have to build it yourself. 🔧 intermediate local transactions give acid : atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability. once data is split across services, each with its own database (as microservices recommend), there is no single transaction manager. options: avoid it: redraw service boundaries so the invariant lives in one service. two-phase commit (strong, blocking). sagas (eventual consistency with compensation). two-phase commit (2pc) two-phase commit: prepare (vote), then commit. 🧠 expert 2pc guarantees atomicity but is blocking : if the coordinator crashes after participants vote yes, they hold locks until it recovers, since they cannot decide alone. latency is at least two round trips with locks held, and availability is the product of every participant’s availability. it works inside a single database vendor’s distributed engine (spanner, cockroachdb run 2pc over raft-replicated groups, so a participant is never really “down”) and in xa transactions acros

topics.title: Resilience: Timeouts, Retries, Backoff, Circuit Breakers, Idempotency
topics.titleHtml: Resilience: Timeouts, Retries, Backoff, Circuit Breakers, Idempotency
topics.search: 👋 intro how to keep a system up when its dependencies fail: timeouts and deadlines, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, idempotency keys, graceful degradation, and chaos engineering. 🌱 beginner everything fails eventually: networks drop packets, servers restart, third parties go down. resilience patterns are the house rules for dealing with it: don’t wait forever (timeouts), try again politely (retries with backoff), stop calling someone who isn’t answering (circuit breaker), and make sure doing something twice is harmless (idempotency). a typical resilience stack around an outbound call. timeouts 🔧 intermediate every network call needs a timeout. without one, a slow dependency ties up threads and connections until your service also stops responding. connect timeout : short (100 ms–1 s). request/read timeout : based on the dependency’s p99.9, plus margin. deadline propagation : pass the remaining time budget downstream (grpc deadlines, a header like x-request-deadline ), so a service does not start work the caller has already given up on. 🧠 expert budgets must shrink down the call tree: if the edge timeout is 2 s, the gateway gives services 1.8 s, and so on. a common bug is an inner timeout larger than the outer one, which makes retries useless. for llm calls use two timeouts: time-to-first-token (e.g. 10 s) and an inter-token idle timeout (e.g. 30 s), rather than one fixed total that would kill long but healthy generations. retries 🔧 int

topics.titleHtml: Storage Engines and Object Storage
heads: Step 2: A Custom Binary Record Format
Range Partitioning vs Consistent Hashing for Storage
topics.search: 👋 intro how data actually gets onto disk and back: the constraints every storage engine faces, building a key-value store step by step (file-backed dictionary, binary format, append-only log, bitcask, lsm tree), immutable versioned files, and the architecture of a large object store such as s3: partitioned metadata, an append-only stream layer, durability through replication and erasure coding, and end-to-end checksums. the constraints 🌱 beginner a disk is like a library where walking to a new shelf is slow but reading along a shelf is fast. good storage engines arrange work so they mostly read and write “along the shelf” (sequentially) and rarely walk around (random access). they also assume the power can be cut at any moment. 🔧 intermediate sequential vs random i/o : sequential writes are far faster than random writes on hdds, and still meaningfully faster on ssds (fewer write amplification effects in the ssd’s own flash translation layer). durability costs fsync : a write in the os page cache is lost on power failure until fsync completes, which can take milliseconds. engines batch many writes per fsync ( group commit ). torn writes : a crash can leave a half-written record. every record needs a length and checksum so recovery can detect and discard it. three amplifications (the rum conjecture: read, update, memory, you can optimize two at the cost of the third): write amplification : bytes written to disk per byte of user data; read amplification : disk reads per lookup;

topics.search: 👋 intro containers and images, kubernetes architecture and core objects, autoscaling, service discovery patterns, service meshes, and running gpu workloads on kubernetes. docker and containers 🌱 beginner before shipping containers, every cargo type needed different handling. the standard steel box changed everything: any crane, ship, or truck can move it. a software container is that box. your app and everything it needs are packed together, so it runs the same on a laptop, a test server, or the cloud. containers share the host kernel, so they start in milliseconds and use far less memory than vms. 🔧 intermediate a container is an isolated process using linux namespaces (what it can see: pids, network, mounts) and cgroups (what it can use: cpu, memory). an image is a stack of read-only layers built from a dockerfile and stored in a registry; standards are defined by the oci. # ---- build stage ---- from golang:1.23 as build workdir /src copy go.mod go.sum ./ run go mod download # cached layer unless deps change copy . . run cgo_enabled=0 go build -o /app ./cmd/server # ---- runtime stage: tiny, no shell, non-root ---- from gcr.io/distroless/static:nonroot copy --from=build /app /app user nonroot:nonroot expose 8080 entrypoint ["/app"] 🧠 expert image hygiene: pin base images by digest, use minimal bases (distroless, chainguard, alpine), order layers from least to most frequently changed, use .dockerignore , run as non-root with a read-only root filesystem, never bake secrets i

topics.search: 👋 intro metrics, logs, and traces with opentelemetry; slos and error budgets; authentication and authorization (oauth 2.x, oidc, jwt); zero trust; secrets; and multi-tenant isolation. observability 🌱 beginner monitoring tells you that the car’s engine light is on. observability lets you figure out why , even for a problem nobody predicted, by looking at the dashboard gauges (metrics), the trip log (logs), and the route you took (traces). opentelemetry as a vendor-neutral pipeline for the three signals. 🔧 intermediate metrics : cheap numeric time series. use red for services (rate, errors, duration) and use for resources (utilization, saturation, errors). avoid high-cardinality labels (user ids). logs : structured json with a trace_id on every line. traces : a tree of spans following one request across services, linked by w3c traceparent headers. sample intelligently (keep all errors and slow requests, a percentage of the rest). profiles : continuous profiling (ebpf-based) is becoming the fourth signal. opentelemetry (otel) is the standard for instrumentation; it includes genai semantic conventions for recording model name, token counts, and latency on llm spans. 🧠 expert slos and error budgets. an slo of 99.9% successful requests over 30 days allows 0.1% failures: the error budget. alert on burn rate , not raw errors: page if the budget burns 14.4 \(\times\) faster than sustainable over 1 hour (2% of budget gone), ticket if 6 \(\times\) over 6 hours. multi-window burn-rate al

topics.titleHtml: GenAI System Design
topics.search: 👋 intro how llm applications are built: tokens and context windows, prompt and context engineering, rag pipelines, embeddings and vector search, agents and tool use (mcp, a2a), llm gateways and model routing, guardrails and prompt-injection defense, evaluation, and cost control. llm basics for system designers 🌱 beginner a large language model is a very well-read autocomplete. given some text, it predicts the next word piece (a token ), adds it, and repeats. it only knows what it learned in training plus what you put in the prompt. it cannot look things up unless you give it tools, and it can sound confident while being wrong. most genai system design is about feeding it the right information and checking what comes out. 🔧 intermediate facts that shape architecture: tokens : about 4 characters or 0.75 english words each. pricing, rate limits, and latency are all per token. output tokens cost 3–5 \(\times\) more than input and are generated one at a time. context window : the maximum tokens per request (input plus output), now commonly 128k to 1m+. bigger contexts cost more, are slower, and models can miss details in the middle. stateless : the api remembers nothing between calls. your system stores conversation history and re-sends what is relevant. non-deterministic : the same input can give different outputs. systems need validation, retries, and evaluations instead of exact tests. latency : time-to-first-token (ttft) plus output length \(\times\) time-per-output-token. str

topics.titleHtml: Inference Engineering
topics.search: 👋 intro what happens inside an llm server: prefill and decode, why decode is memory-bound, kv cache math, continuous batching, pagedattention, prefix caching, chunked prefill, disaggregated serving, quantization, speculative decoding, parallelism strategies, serving engines, metrics, and autoscaling. how generation works 🌱 beginner reading the question is fast: the model reads all words of your prompt at once, in parallel. writing the answer is slow: it must write one token, then reread its notes to write the next, and so on. to avoid rereading everything each time, it keeps a notebook of what it has already processed. that notebook is the kv cache , and managing it is most of inference engineering. the two phases of llm inference. 🔧 intermediate prefill : process the whole prompt in one forward pass, producing the first token and filling the kv cache. large matrix multiplies, so it is compute-bound . determines time-to-first-token (ttft) . decode : generate one token per forward pass, reading all model weights and the kv cache each step. very little compute per byte read, so it is memory-bandwidth-bound . determines time per output token (tpot) , also called inter-token latency (itl). end-to-end latency \(\approx\) ttft \(+\) tpot \(\times\) (output tokens \(-1\) ). the roofline: why batching matters roofline for an h100-class gpu (approximate figures). decode at batch 1 uses a tiny fraction of the gpu’s compute. 🧠 expert during decode, each weight (2 bytes in bf16) is used

topics.titleHtml: Real-World Case Studies: Real-Time and Messaging
topics.search: 👋 intro eight systems that move messages to millions of connected clients or between thousands of services: slack, whatsapp, discord, netflix, linkedin, facebook live, mcdonald’s, and uber. the common thread. real-time systems split into a stateful edge that holds connections and a stateless or sharded core that decides where messages go. almost every case below has a connection layer, a routing layer based on consistent hashing, and a fan-out step. the hard problems are reconnect storms, hot channels, and knowing where each user is connected. case: slack: the journey of a message 📋 case facts domain: workplace chat scale: tens of millions of channels per host; about 500 ms global delivery concepts: websockets, consistent hashing, stateful services, regional edges, presence source: slack engineering blog, “real-time messaging” (2023) slack’s real-time path: send via http, fan out via websockets. the components. channel servers (cs) are stateful, in-memory java services holding recent history for channels. each cs owns a set of channels via consistent hashing ; at peak a host serves about 16 million channels. “channel” is abstract: a user, a team, a file, a huddle, or a regular channel. charms (consistent hash ring managers) keep the ring healthy and replace a failed cs in under 20 seconds. ring configuration lives in consul. gateway servers (gs) hold each user’s websocket and its channel subscriptions. they are the only part deployed in many regions, so users connect nearby.

topics.search: 👋 intro ten systems that serve content to huge audiences: twitter’s timelines and recommendations, youtube, netflix (cdn, cache, api), dropbox, reddit, stack overflow, and the real-time collaboration engines behind google docs and figma. the common thread. content systems are read-heavy by orders of magnitude. the central design question is when to do the work : at write time (precompute feeds, transcode every format) or at read time (assemble on demand). the answer is almost always “precompute for the common case, compute on demand for the expensive outliers.” case: twitter: timelines and the fan-out problem 📋 case facts domain: social media scale: about 300k timeline reads/s vs about 6k tweet writes/s (2012–2013 talks) concepts: fan-out on write, redis timelines, hybrid push/pull, celebrity problem source: raffi krikorian, “timelines at scale”, qcon 2012 the numbers that drive the design. reads outnumber writes by about 50:1. users expect their home timeline instantly. so twitter did the work at write time. fan-out on write. when a user tweets, a fan-out service looks up their followers and inserts the tweet id into each follower’s home timeline, stored as a list in a redis cluster (replicated three times). only ids are stored (plus a little metadata), and only the latest few hundred entries per user. reading a timeline is then one redis read followed by a multi-get of tweet bodies from a tweet store and cache. users who have not logged in for a while are not fanned out to;

topics.search: 👋 intro the algorithms behind modern models, at the level research engineers and ai engineers are asked to implement and reason about: backpropagation, optimizers, normalization and initialization, convolution and nms, attention and its variants, positional encodings (rope), the online softmax behind flashattention, kv caching, decoding strategies, speculative decoding, contrastive and preference losses (infonce, dpo, ppo, grpo), lora, quantization, vector search (hnsw, ivf-pq), and distributed training. backpropagation 🌱 beginner a factory produces a bad product. to fix it, trace backward: how much did the last machine contribute to the defect, and how much did each earlier machine contribute through it? backpropagation does exactly that with derivatives, reusing each machine’s answer instead of recomputing it. reverse-mode automatic differentiation forward: evaluate operations in topological order, recording each node’s inputs (the tape) \(\bar{l} \gets 1\) ; all other gradients \(\gets 0\) for each node \(v\) in reverse topological order do for each input \(u\) of \(v\) do \(\bar u \gets \bar u + \bar v \cdot \partial v/\partial u\) ▷ chain rule; accumulate over all uses end end ❓ why reverse order guarantees that when \(v\) is processed, \(\bar v\) already includes the contributions of every node that uses \(v\) . the cost is a small constant times the forward pass, regardless of the number of parameters, which is why reverse mode (not forward mode) is used for scalar los

topics.search: 👋 intro how low-level (object-oriented) design rounds and multi-part “practical coding” rounds work, the principles and patterns that score well, a concurrency primer, and complete designs for classic problems (lru cache, rate limiter, key-value store with transactions and ttl, task scheduler, pub/sub) and ml-flavored problems (dynamic batching inference server, feature store, tool executor for agents, experiment tracker). what the round looks like 🌱 beginner a system design round asks “which boxes and arrows?” a low-level design round asks “which classes, methods, and data structures inside one box?” it is closer to real day-to-day engineering: clean interfaces that are easy to extend when the interviewer adds a new requirement every ten minutes. 🔧 intermediate typical flow (45–60 minutes): clarify requirements and the api (5 min). write the public interface first. identify entities, responsibilities, and relationships (5–10 min). choose data structures and complexities for each operation. implement the core path (20 min), with tests. extensions arrive: “now add ttl,” “now make it thread-safe,” “now persist it,” “now support transactions.” good structure makes each one small. scoring: correctness, api clarity, separation of concerns, extensibility, testing, handling of edge cases and concurrency, and explaining trade-offs. principles that interviewers look for 🔧 intermediate single responsibility : a class has one reason to change (eviction policy separate from storage). ope

topics.search: 👋 intro several hundred questions and problems of the kinds commonly reported in ml engineer, ai engineer, applied scientist, research engineer, and research scientist interviews, grouped by round. conceptual and scenario questions come with short answer sketches that point to the chapter with the full explanation. problem lists name the pattern so you can practice recognizing it. how to use this chapter. cover the answer sketch and answer out loud first, as you would in a round. a good answer states the core idea in one or two sentences, then gives the trade-off, a failure case, and an example. sketches here are deliberately short; if yours is much shorter or misses the trade-off, reread the referenced chapter. these are representative question types , not a claim that a particular company asks a particular question; loops change, so check recent reports for your target company. ml fundamentals (breadth round) explain the bias–variance trade-off. how do you tell which one you have? answer sketch: error = bias \(^2\) + variance + noise. high training error means bias; a large train–validation gap means variance. learning curves show whether more data helps (ch. 17). l1 vs l2 regularization: what does each do, and why does l1 give sparse weights? answer sketch: l2 shrinks all weights (gaussian prior); l1 pushes some exactly to zero (laplace prior) because its penalty has a corner at zero, so the optimum often lands on an axis. why is logistic regression trained with cross-entr
